extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of classical history; editors and translators preparing editions; Project Gutenberg users/distributors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary on selecting, translating, and presenting excerpts from classical historical works (Tacitus), plus the Project Gutenberg redistribution and licensing requirements for distributing the electronic text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unity of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection should maintain the unity of the volume's purpose — in this case, to present the history of Tiberius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit material that does not serve the selected unity; choose passages so the volume 'shall present the history of Tiberius.' The editor states he has 'endeavoured so to guide my choice, that it shall present the history of Tiberius.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain chapters preserving actions or sayings of the principal subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When omitting parts of a larger work, retain every chapter which preserves an action or a saying of the central figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor: 'I have omitted some chapters, which describe criminal events and legal tragedies in Rome: but of these, I have retained every chapter, which preserves an action or a saying of Tiberius; and what I have inserted is a sufficient specimen of the remainder.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit wearisome or irrelevant content
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude chapters occupied with tedious or obscure material that detracts from the volume's focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: omit 'wearisome disputes between the Royal Houses of Parthia and Armenia' and tedious regional rebellions (e.g., Tacfarinas) when they do not contribute to the chosen theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and respect the translator/editor's work (do not mangle the translator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not abridge or alter a translator's rendering in a way that misrepresents or 'mangles' their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor says: 'It is not my purpose here to abridge Tacitus, to mangle his translator, nor to try and say what is better said in the body of the volume.' Maintain fidelity to translator where possible; indicate editorial interventions transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient specimen of omitted material
rubrics_metrics.description: When omitting large parts, include representative specimens so readers have an idea of the omitted content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor claims what is inserted is 'a sufficient specimen of the remainder.' Use representative excerpts rather than wholesale omission without illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about omissions and editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear which chapters or passages have been left out and why, so scholarly readers can perceive omissions and other readers are not misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor notes: 'the chapters are not numbered: for the omission, I am not responsible; and I can only lament, what I may not control. But scholars, who know their Tacitus, will perceive what I have left out.' Explicit editorial notes and introductions should explain selection decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate historical claims by evidence, avoid supplying unproven motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Historians should be cautious about supplying motives and passing judgment without sufficient evidence; evidence that would satisfy a court may be required for strong accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary: 'Tacitus supplies motives to them, and then passes judgment upon his own assumptions: that the evidence ... would hardly be accepted in a court of law.' Prefer to record actions and sayings rather than infer definitive motives from rumor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of concision and precision in historical prose
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality historical writing is marked by expressive conciseness and 'precision about [the] words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praises of Tacitus: 'for wisdom and force,' 'a great purist, and affected a wonderful precision about his words,' and Gibbon's 'expressive conciseness.' Use clear, concise phrasing and carefully chosen words in translations and editorial prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present balanced portrait by including favourable and unfavourable evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When characterizing historical figures, include both positive and negative accounts, and consider contradictory authoritative sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor balances Tacitus, Suetonius, and Velleius Paterculus; notes 'The two best authorities contradict one another' and argues readers should weigh conflicting testimony rather than accept a single depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve notable subsidiary works in full when they are of distinct interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Include complete minor works that are entertaining or of special interest (e.g., 'The Account of Germany' and 'The Life of Agricola').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor included these works in full because they are 'entertaining, and should have a particular interest for English readers.' Favor completeness for standalone pieces with distinct value.
